title: Boolean
body:
`bool`. Holds `true` or `false`, nothing else. An [[Atomic type]].

```c++
bool found = false;
cout << found;         // prints 0, not "false"
cout << boolalpha << found;   // prints false
```

C++ treats zero as false and every non-zero value as true, which is why `if (x = 0)`
compiles and is always false: it assigns, then tests the result. That is the classic
[[Logic Errors|logic error]].

One byte, even though one bit would do. See [[Boolean Representation]] in
[[COMPUTING MACHINERY]] for why, and [[Conditional]] for where booleans get used.
